description:
We are building for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, which is about creating an easy tool that shows Sun and Earth positions at Moon south pole landing sites, so planners can compare sites and dates for power and Earth communication.

We have the software side covered. We are looking for:

a physics, astrophysics, or engineering student to help check our Sun and Earth geometry.
summary:
Moon Maps, by team Lunar Titans, is a web app that tells mission planners, educators and the public whether a place on the Moon is a good landing site at a given time. A lander needs sunlight for power and the Earth in view for a direct radio link. For any point and moment, Moon Maps computes where the Sun and the Earth are in the sky and whether each is above the real terrain horizon, using NASA JPL's DE421 ephemeris and NASA's LOLA elevation maps.

Users can spin a 3D Moon and land anywhere to watch the Sun and Earth rise over the skyline, get a verdict and a 30-day calendar of good landing windows, compare sites and dates by switching between them, and explore 17 curated sites, including Artemis candidate regions and Apollo landings. A chat assistant answers questions using only numbers from the Moon Maps API, and shows its sources.

Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons within 0.0001°. Over 18.6 years at 300 south pole points, the results match NASA Goddard's polar maps with correlations of 0.992 for sunlight and 0.999 for Earth visibility.
details:
What it does

Moon Maps (https://moonmaps.vercel.app) tells you whether a place on the Moon, at a chosen time, is good for landing. A lander needs two things: sunlight for its solar panels, and the Earth in view for a direct radio link. For any point and moment, Moon Maps computes where the Sun and the Earth are in the sky and checks whether each one is above the real terrain horizon. When both are, the site is good.

How it works

Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL's DE421 ephemeris. The horizon comes from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation maps: 80 m and 120 m grids at the south pole, and a global grid everywhere else. Users can land anywhere on a 3D Moon and watch the Sun and Earth rise over the real skyline. The planner gives a clear verdict and a 30-day calendar of good landing windows, and changing the site or date updates the answer at once. Each of the 17 curated sites (Artemis candidate regions, Apollo landings and other missions) has a 14-day sky forecast, a horizon panorama, an elevation map, the distance to Earth, and when to leave Earth to land in the next good window. A chat assistant explains the results, using only numbers it gets from our API.

Benefits and impact

Tools such as JPL Horizons and Moon Trek are built for detailed analysis. Moon Maps answers the planning question in seconds and in plain words. When a launch slips, a team can quickly see how a new date or a nearby site changes power and communication. Students and the public can see why the lunar south pole is so hard: the Sun stays low and hills can hide it.

Accuracy

Our Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons within 0.0001°. Our Sun angles match JPL Horizons at 16 Apollo moonwalk times. Over 18.6 years at 300 south pole points, our results match NASA Goddard's polar maps with a correlation of 0.992 for sunlight and 0.999 for Earth visibility.

Tools

  • API: Python, FastAPI, Skyfield and NumPy.
  • Web app: TypeScript, Next.js, React, three.js, Tailwind CSS and GSAP.
  • Hosting and workflow: Vercel hosts both parts. GitHub Actions runs 290 automated tests on every change. Jira holds the task board.
  • Chat: free AI model providers.

Creativity

  • Landed view: you see the real horizon from where you stand.
  • Planning tools: a weather-style forecast for the Sun and Earth, and departure times based on real past missions.
  • Assistant: it is not allowed to invent numbers.

Factors we considered

  • The Moon has no atmosphere, so the terrain alone sets the horizon.
  • Near the south pole the Sun skims the horizon.
  • The Moon's slow wobble makes the Earth rise and set there.
  • Small moves in place or time can change the answer.
  • We consider accuracy against NASA sources, accessibility (keyboard, phones, reduced motion), citing every source, and the judges' feedback, which we acted on during the event
